articles.title: Biochemical Profiles, DPPH Radical-Scavenging Activity, and Associated Soil Properties of WildL. andL. Populations in Southeastern Bulgaria

1. Introduction

The genusL. (Rubiaceae) comprises a taxonomically diverse group of herbaceous species characterized by extensive geographical distribution, high ecological plasticity, and pronounced variation in habitat requirements. Recognized as the largest and one of the most widely distributed genera within the tribe Rubieae,includes species adapted to a broad spectrum of environmental conditions, ranging from semi-natural ecosystems to highly disturbed habitats [,,]. In particular,has been documented from diverse lowland and disturbed habitats across Europe, whereashas been reported from mountains, grasslands, meadows, river beaches, open fields, ditch sides, streamsides, wet places, forests, thickets, and valleys over a broad elevational range extending from near sea level to 4100 m. This ecological diversity highlights the suitability offor investigating associations between habitat-specific environmental conditions, plant nutritional status, and metabolic variability [,].

Among the species examined in the present study,anddiffer in life history and habitat occupancy.is a perennial taxon occurring across diverse open and semi-open environments.is an annual climbing or scrambling herb that often colonizes nutrient-enriched or disturbed sites and can exploit surrounding vegetation as physical support [,,].

The phytochemical importance ofhas been emphasized in recent reviews summarizing its diverse bioactive constituents []. To complement these insights, foundational historical works and older screening literature have long established the basic qualitative chemical framework of the genus [,], while more recent investigations have confirmed the occurrence of flavonoids, phenolic acids, iridoids, anthraquinones, steroids, and other specialized metabolites in the genus, together with antioxidant and other biological activities [,]. A 2025 phytochemical study ofdocumented multiple compound classes of chemotaxonomic relevance, including flavonoids, phenolic acids, an iridoid, anthraquinones, nucleosides, and steroids []. Comparative studies involvingandhave demonstrated species-related differences in phenolic composition, flavonoid abundance, and antioxidant potential []. These two species were therefore selected because their taxonomic relatedness, occurrence within the same broad floristic regions of Bulgaria, contrasting life histories and habitat affinities, and documented phytochemical relevance provide a focused framework for comparing their biochemical profiles in relation to associated soil properties.

Nevertheless, phytochemical diversity among natural populations is unlikely to be determined exclusively by genetic background, as environmental conditions may substantially modify metabolite accumulation within and among species. Increasing evidence from medicinal plant research indicates that plants growing under different light regimes, moisture conditions, soil reaction, and nutrient supply may express substantially altered biochemical profiles, even when they belong to the same species [].

In this context, edaphic factors are especially important because they simultaneously influence mineral nutrition, osmotic balance, rhizosphere interactions, and enzymatic processes linked to primary and secondary metabolism. Soil pH affects nutrient solubility and availability [,], whereas phosphorus (P) is central to phosphate homeostasis and energy-related metabolism [,]. Sulfur (S) is integral to core metabolic processes and stress-related biochemical functions []. Zinc (Zn) and copper (Cu) are essential micronutrients that serve as structural or catalytic cofactors in numerous proteins and enzymes involved in plant metabolism and stress responses [,,]. Soil organic matter (OM) contributes to nutrient retention, water-holding capacity, aggregate stability, and microbial activity [,]. The contrasting ecological strategies ofandmay be associated with differences in nutrient acquisition, responses to environmental stress, and specialized metabolite profiles [,,,]. Therefore, an integrated analysis of plant and soil composition can support a more comprehensive interpretation of naturally occurring biochemical variability [,].

Previous phytochemical studies ofandhave reported radical-scavenging or antioxidant responses of their extracts [,]. In the present study, the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) assay was selected as a comparative in vitro screening measure of the radical-scavenging activity of crude methanolic extracts. Because it represents a single chemical assay, it was not intended to provide a comprehensive assessment of antioxidant capacity or to demonstrate biological efficacy or a specific practical application. Environmental factors, including soil properties, climatic conditions, and abiotic stress, can alter the accumulation of secondary metabolites and the biochemical characteristics of plant material [,,,,]. Consequently, the absence of corresponding soil characterization may limit the ecological interpretation of biochemical differences associated with species identity, environmental variation, or both [].

The present study integrates plant and soil analyses from six defined sampling points in Bulgaria. One population of each species was sampled in each of the Eastern Stara Planina, Thracian Lowland, and Tundzha Hilly Plain floristic regions. These sites represent distinct ecological contexts, including open field margins, river-associated habitats, shrub-dominated habitats, and soils differing in texture, nutrient availability, and pH. This sampling framework allowed biochemical and edaphic variation to be described across the six sampling points within a geographically constrained but environmentally heterogeneous study area. However, it was not designed to separate the independent effects of species identity, sampling site, collection period, and associated soil conditions.

Based on the ecological and edaphic contrasts among the studied sites, we hypothesized that the sampled populations ofandwould exhibit differing biochemical profiles and that site-specific soil characteristics, particularly pH and micronutrient availability, would be associated with variation in DPPH radical-scavenging activity and proximate composition.

Accordingly, the aim of the present study was to characterize the proximate composition, phytochemical content, and DPPH radical-scavenging activity of six wild populations offrom southeastern Bulgaria and to examine these traits in relation to the associated soil properties. By linking plant chemical profiles with environmental measurements, this study provides ecological context for biochemical variability inandunder natural field conditions.

The specific objectives were: (i) to summarize the analytical profiles of each sampling point; (ii) to provide a descriptive comparison of the mean compositional and phytochemical characteristics and DPPH radical-scavenging activity of theandsamples; (iii) to describe the chemical and textural properties of the soils associated with each sampling point; and (iv) to explore multivariate patterns and site-level soil–plant associations using principal component analysis (PCA) and exact-permutation Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. These objectives provide a framework for describing biochemical and edaphic variation among the six sampled populations and for generating hypotheses to be tested in larger, balanced studies.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Study Area and Plant Material

Wild populations ofL. andL. were collected from six distinct sampling points located within three floristic regions of Bulgaria: the Eastern Stara Planina, Thracian Lowland, and Tundzha Hilly Plain regions. Three populations were sampled for each species, with each population representing an independent field location characterized by specific ecological and edaphic conditions. The selected sites represented contrasting habitats, including open field margins, river-associated habitats, and shrub-dominated vegetation, and differed in soil texture, nutrient availability, and soil reaction. The geographic location, altitude, and floristic affiliation of the six sampling points (P1-P6) are presented in. The corresponding sampling-site data are also provided in.

Aerial plant parts were collected at full flowering on 9 May 2025 at P4, 17 May 2025 at P5, and 18 May 2025 at P6 for, and on 16 June 2025 at P1, 27 June 2025 at P2, and 29 June 2025 at P3 for. The difference in collection dates reflected differences in the timing of full flowering between the two species under local field conditions. Consequently, the collection period was completely aligned with species identity, and potential seasonal influences could not be distinguished from the biochemical differences between the two groups of samples. The collected plant material consisted of apical shoot portions approximately 30–40 cm long, which were cut with scissors above ground level so that the roots were excluded. The samples included stems bearing leaves and reproductive structures (flowers and, where present, developing fruits). Although sampling was standardized by the approximate length of the collected shoot portions, the relative proportions of stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits were not separately quantified. Plant identification was performed using standard taxonomic keys and authoritative floristic references for the Bulgarian flora [,]. Following collection, the plant material was transported to the laboratory and processed as described in.

2.2. Soil Sampling

Root-zone soil samples associated with each studied plant population were collected during the same field campaign as the corresponding plant material to ensure direct soil–plant correspondence. At each site, soil material was collected from a depth of 0–30 cm using a soil probe. Sampling followed the general representative-sampling principles recommended by Lancrop Laboratories (Pocklington, UK), including transect-based collection and preparation of a composite sample from multiple subsamples. For each population, 15–20 individual cores (subsamples) were collected along a zigzag transect, depending on the spatial extent of the plant population. The subsamples were then pooled, thoroughly mixed, and homogenized to obtain one representative composite sample per site. The final mass of each composite soil sample ranged from 600 to 800 g. Before dispatch to the laboratory, the samples were air-dried, cleaned of stones and plant debris, gently crushed, double-bagged, labeled, and transported by express courier to Lancrop Laboratories for analysis.

2.3. Soil Analysis

Soil analyses were performed by Lancrop Laboratories (Pocklington, UK), a laboratory holding United Kingdom Accreditation Service (UKAS) accreditation for specified testing activities. The composite soil samples were air-dried before analysis, as described in. The analytical dataset included soil pH, organic matter, cation exchange capacity (CEC), plant-available macroelements and microelements, and particle-size distribution, including sand, silt, and clay fractions.

Soil pH was determined using the Macauley method, with calcium chloride (CaCl) as the extractant. Soil organic matter was determined by loss on ignition (LOI) at 500 °C. Plant-available phosphorus was extracted using the Olsen method with sodium hydrogen carbonate and determined by discrete colorimetric analysis following reaction with ammonium molybdate. Plant-available sulfur was extracted using calcium tetrahydrogen diorthophosphate and determined by inductively coupled plasma (ICP) analysis. Plant-available copper and zinc were extracted with 0.05 M disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetate (EDTA) and determined by ICP analysis. Cation exchange capacity was determined after rinsing the soil with water and subsequent leaching with 1 M ammonium acetate, followed by ICP analysis.

Particle-size distribution was determined by Lancrop Laboratories as part of its soil-texture analysis service and was reported as percentages of sand, silt, and clay, together with the corresponding soil-texture classification. The specific documented in-house procedure used for particle-size determination was not provided in the analytical report or in the publicly available laboratory documentation.

These variables were used to characterize soil fertility, nutrient availability, and textural class at each sampling point, and subsequently to explore their potential associations with the biochemical traits of the studiedpopulations.

2.4. Preparation of Plant Material

The harvested aerial plant material was manually cleaned without washing to remove visible soil particles and foreign material. Samples from both species were then dried for five days under identical ambient laboratory conditions (18–20 °C). The material was spread in a thin layer in a dark, well-ventilated area and turned daily to promote uniform drying. The same drying procedure was applied to both species, despite their collection in different months. After drying, the material was ground to a fine homogeneous powder (particle size < 400 µm) using a laboratory mill. The powdered samples were stored under dry, light-protected conditions until further analysis. Standardized powdered material was subsequently used for proximate analyses and ultrasound-assisted methanolic extraction.

2.5. Preparation of Methanolic Extracts and Determination of Dry Extract

Methanolic extracts were prepared from the dried and powdered aerial parts of the studiedspecies using 99.9% methanol at a ratio of 1 g plant material to 10 mL solvent. Ultrasound-assisted extraction was performed for 30 min at room temperature using an Elmasonic S30 ultrasonic bath (Elma Schmidbauer GmbH, Singen, Germany) operating at a frequency of 37 kHz and a nominal effective ultrasonic power of 80 W. The resulting extracts were filtered through laboratory-grade filter paper to remove suspended plant particles.

The dry-extract concentration of each methanolic extract was determined gravimetrically by evaporating a 0.5 mL aliquot to dryness and calculating the mass of the resulting residue per milliliter of extract. Dry-extract yield was expressed as a percentage of the initial dry plant mass.

Based on the gravimetrically determined concentration, a working solution containing 1.0 mg dry extract/mL was prepared from each extract by dilution with methanol. For each sampling period, the working solutions were subsequently used for the phytochemical and DPPH radical-scavenging analyses on the day of preparation, without prolonged storage. The quantitative spectrophotometric results were calculated on a dry-extract basis and expressed per gram of dry extract.

2.6. Proximate Composition

The plant material was analyzed for moisture, dry matter, crude protein, crude fiber, crude fat, ash, and nitrogen-free extract (NFE) at the Central Scientific Research Laboratory, Trakia University (Stara Zagora, Bulgaria), which is accredited in accordance with BDS EN ISO/IEC 17025:2018 []. According to the official laboratory information, the laboratory applies methods established in international, regional, and Bulgarian standards in its analytical activities. The directly measured proximate-composition parameters were determined in duplicate (= 2 analytical determinations) using the single pooled plant sample from each sampling point, and the results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Dry matter was calculated as 100 − moisture, whereas NFE was calculated by difference. All proximate-composition results were expressed as percentages.

2.6.1. Determination of Moisture and Dry Matter

Moisture content was determined gravimetrically following the protocol of BDS ISO 6496:2000 []. Dry matter content was calculated as the difference from 100%.

2.6.2. Determination of Crude Protein

Crude protein content was calculated based on the obtained values of total nitrogen content, which was determined using the Kjeldahl method according to BDS ISO 5983-1:2006 []. The procedure included mineralization with sulfuric acid, followed by ammonia distillation and titrimetric determination.

2.6.3. Determination of Crude Fat

Crude fat content was determined according to the procedure described in BDS ISO 6492:2007 []. The method involves Soxhlet extraction using an organic solvent and gravimetric determination of the extracted residue.

Crude fiber content was determined using an in-house validated method (IVM 3/2024) based on BDS EN ISO 6865:2001 []. The method includes sequential acid and alkaline hydrolysis with intermediate filtration, followed by washing, drying, and gravimetric determination of the remaining insoluble fibrous residue. The results were expressed as a percentage of the initial sample mass.

2.6.6. Determination of Ash Content

Crude ash content was determined in accordance with ISO 5984:2022 [] by incineration of samples until complete removal of organic matter, with the resulting mineral residue determined gravimetrically.

2.7. Spectrophotometric Biochemical Analyses of the Studied Plants

All spectrophotometric measurements were performed by the authors using an ONDA TOUCH UV-31 SCAN ultraviolet-visible spectrophotometer (GIORGIO BORMAC SRL, Modena, Italy). The DPPH, TPC, and TFC assays were based on the protocols described by Memdueva et al. [].

All spectrophotometric assays were performed using freshly prepared methanolic working solutions adjusted to a dry-extract concentration of 1.0 mg/mL. For each assay, the absorbance of each independently prepared analytical sample was recorded once at each wavelength required by the corresponding method; no repeated instrumental readings of the same reaction mixture were performed.

2.7.1. Determination of DPPH Radical-Scavenging Activity

DPPH radical-scavenging activity was evaluated using the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical-scavenging assay. Briefly, 100 µL of the working extract solution was mixed with 3.9 mL of 0.1 mM methanolic DPPH solution. After 30 min of incubation in the dark at room temperature, the decrease in absorbance was measured spectrophotometrically at λ = 517 nm. The results were calculated as percentage inhibition according to the standard relationship between control absorbance and sample absorbance. DPPH radical-scavenging activity was also expressed as micromoles of Trolox equivalents per gram of dry extract (µmol TE/g DE) using Trolox standard solutions for calibration over the concentration range of 5–50 µmol/L (R= 0.9991).

2.7.2. Determination of Total Phenolic Content

Total phenolic content (TPC) was determined using the Folin–Ciocalteu method. A 0.5 mL aliquot of the working extract solution was mixed with 2.5 mL of Folin–Ciocalteu reagent diluted 1:10 (/) with deionized water. Subsequently, 2.0 mL of 7.5% (/) NaCOsolution was added. After incubation for 60 min at room temperature, the absorbance was measured spectrophotometrically at λ = 765 nm. Gallic acid was used as the calibration standard over the concentration range of 10–150 µg/mL, and the total phenolic content was calculated from the corresponding calibration curve (R= 0.9996). The results were expressed as milligrams of gallic acid equivalents per gram of dry extract (mg GAE/g DE).

2.7.3. Determination of Total Flavonoid Content

Total flavonoid content (TFC) was determined using the aluminum chloride colorimetric method. Briefly, 1.0 mL of the working extract solution was mixed with 4.0 mL of deionized water and 0.3 mL of 5% (/) NaNOsolution. After 5 min, 0.3 mL of 10% (/) AlClsolution was added. After an additional 6 min, 2.0 mL of 1 M NaOH was added. The mixture was homogenized, and the absorbance was measured spectrophotometrically at 510 nm. Catechin was used as the calibration standard over the concentration range of 10–150 mg/L, and the total flavonoid content was calculated from the corresponding calibration curve (R= 0.9997). The results were expressed as milligrams of catechin equivalents per gram of dry extract (mg CE/g DE).

2.7.4. pH-Differential Anthocyanin Assay

Total anthocyanin content (TAntC) was determined spectrophotometrically using the pH differential method described by Lee et al. [], with modifications. Briefly, separate 2.0 mL aliquots of each working extract solution were mixed with 8.0 mL of 0.025 M potassium chloride buffer (pH 1.0) and 8.0 mL of 0.4 M sodium acetate buffer (pH 4.5), respectively. The calculated assay responses, expressed as milligrams of cyanidin-3-glucoside equivalents per gram of dry extract (mg CGE/g DE), are retained in thefor transparency.

2.8. Replication and Data Structure

A total of six sampling points, each representing a distinct field population, were included in the study. At each sampling point, the collected plant material was combined into one pooled sample. For each spectrophotometric assay, three analytical samples were independently prepared from the pooled plant material and analyzed separately. The directly measured proximate-composition parameters were determined in duplicate (= 2 analytical determinations), whereas dry matter and NFE were calculated variables. DPPH radical-scavenging activity (expressed as both Trolox equivalents and percentage inhibition), TPC, and TFC were treated quantitatively, whereas the anthocyanin assay responses were interpreted qualitatively, as described in. The analytical samples were neither repeated measurements of the same extract nor independent biological samples. Accordingly, they quantified analytical variability only, and the resulting means and standard deviations do not estimate within-population biological variability. One corresponding soil sample was analyzed for each sampling point, providing six matched site-level soil–plant datasets. These datasets allowed an exploratory examination of covariation between plant biochemical traits and associated soil properties; however, the design did not permit the effects of species, site, collection period, and edaphic conditions to be separated.

2.9. Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize plant biochemical traits and soil properties at each sampling point. For moisture, crude protein, crude fiber, crude fat, and ash, point-level means and standard deviations were based on two analytical determinations (= 2); dry matter and NFE were calculated variables. For DPPH radical-scavenging activity, expressed as both Trolox equivalents and percentage inhibition, TPC, and TFC, each point-level mean was based on three independently prepared analytical samples obtained from the single pooled plant sample collected at that sampling point. Accordingly, the associated standard deviations characterize analytical variability rather than within-population biological variability. The anthocyanin assay responses were interpreted qualitatively and were not included in quantitative descriptive summaries, PCA, or Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. For the descriptive summaries calculated separately for each species, arithmetic means and standard deviations were calculated across the three corresponding point-level values. These summaries were not treated as estimates of an independent species effect, and no inferential comparison between species was performed because species identity was confounded with sampling site, collection period, and associated soil conditions.

Multivariate relationships among the studied variables were examined using principal component analysis, which was applied to visualize the distribution of the six sampling points according to their biochemical and edaphic profiles. Prior to PCA, all variables were standardized (scaled to unit variance) to minimize the influence of differing measurement scales. The PCA was performed using selected plant and soil variables summarized for each sampling point. The plant variables included crude protein, ash, nitrogen-free extract, crude fat, DPPH radical-scavenging activity, percentage inhibition, total phenolic content, and total flavonoid content. The soil variables included organic matter, pH, cation exchange capacity, phosphorus, sulfur, copper, zinc, sand content, and clay content. These variables were selected to represent the principal patterns in proximate composition, DPPH radical-scavenging activity, phytochemical content, and edaphic properties within the limited set of matched sampling points.

To explore potential associations between soil properties and plant biochemical traits, Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was performed at the sampling-point level. This nonparametric approach was selected because of the small sample size and the exploratory nature of the dataset. Correlations were calculated using one matched soil dataset and one point-level plant dataset per sampling point (= 6). For each soil–plant variable pair, a two-sided exact permutation-value was calculated as the proportion of all 720 possible permutations that produced an absolute Spearman correlation coefficient at least as large as the absolute observed coefficient. Nominal, unadjusted-values were reported, with< 0.05 used as an exploratory reporting criterion rather than as confirmatory evidence. The Cu concentration at P4 was reported by the analytical laboratory as >100 ppm. For PCA and Spearman’s rank correlation analysis, this above-range result was assigned the boundary value of 100 ppm. This substitution preserved the rank order of the Cu values in Spearman’s analysis because P4 remained the highest-ranked observation; however, the contribution of Cu to the PCA was interpreted cautiously because PCA is sensitive to numerical magnitude. A heatmap of the resulting Spearman correlation matrix was prepared in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA) solely to visualize the results; no statistical calculations were performed in Excel.

Descriptive analyses and PCA were performed using jamovi (version 2.7.38) []. The PCA implementation used the R statistical environment (version 4.5) [] and the FactoMineR package [,]. Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients and their two-sided exact permutation-values were calculated using R code executed through the Rj Editor within jamovi. Given the limited number of sampling points, the results of all statistical analyses were interpreted as exploratory. They were used to identify general patterns of variation and potential soil–plant associations and were not interpreted as evidence of causal relationships.

3. Results

The results are presented in a structured manner, including characterization of soil physicochemical properties across the six sampling sites, evaluation of proximate composition of aerial plant biomass, assessment of antioxidant and phytochemical characteristics, species-level comparison of the studied taxa, multivariate ordination based on PCA, and exploratory analysis of soil–plant associations.

3.1. Soil Characteristics of the Studied Populations

The six sampling points differed in their chemical and physical soil properties, confirming the edaphic heterogeneity of the studied habitats. Organic matter content ranged from the lowest value of 1.7% at P3 (, Banya) to the highest value of 10.3% at P5 (, Tselina). Soil reaction also varied substantially, from pH 6.3 at P1 (, Blyagornitsa) to pH 8.1 at P4 (, Banya), indicating a gradient from slightly acidic to alkaline conditions.

The soils associated withwere generally richer in several plant-available nutrients than those associated with. P ranged from 67 to 323 ppm at thesites, compared with 9 to 13 ppm at thesites. A similar trend was observed for S, with values of 15–45 ppm insites versus 3–6 ppm insites. Zn concentrations also tended to be higher in thesoils, reaching 175 ppm at P5, whereas the lowest value (13.7 ppm) was recorded at P2 (, Malka Vereya). Cu showed strong site-to-site variability, with the highest reported value at P4 (), where the laboratory report indicated a concentration above 100 ppm.

Soil texture also differed among the sampling points. P2, P3, and P4 were classified as clay loam, P5 as sandy loam, and P1 and P6 as sandy silt loam. Sand content ranged from 24.3% at P2 to 55.4% at P5, whereas clay content ranged from 7.09% at P5 to 26.1% at P2. Cation exchange capacity varied between 17.5 and 28.4 meq/100 g, with the highest value recorded at P6 ().

The measured soil properties varied among the sampling points in terms of organic matter status, soil reaction, nutrient availability, and texture, providing a heterogeneous edaphic background for the investigated plant populations. 3.3. Phytochemical Content and DPPH Radical-Scavenging Activity

The analyses of phytochemical content and DPPH radical-scavenging activity revealed variation among the six sampled populations and between the two groups of species-associated samples. At the sampling-point level, DPPH radical-scavenging activity ranged from 13.2 ± 1.7 µmol TE/g DE at P4 () to 27.1 ± 3.5 µmol TE/g DE at P2 (). The percentage inhibition in the DPPH assay followed the same general pattern, with the highest point-level mean value observed at P1 (; 50.4 ± 2.3%) and the lowest at P4 (; 20.4 ± 1.1%).

Total phenolic content (TPC) ranged from 48.6 ± 3.3 mg GAE/g DE at P1 () to 65.2 ± 12.4 mg GAE/g DE at P4 (). Total flavonoid content (TFC) varied within a narrower interval, from 40.6 ± 1.4 mg CE/g DE at P6 () to 49.4 ± 8.0 mg CE/g DE at P1 (). The pH-differential assay produced only trace-level anthocyanin responses, with generally higher signals in thesamples than in thesamples. Because matrix-specific limits of detection and quantification were not established and the lowest responses showed high analytical variability, the anthocyanin results were interpreted qualitatively rather than as reliable quantitative measurements.

When the three sampling-point means were averaged for each species, the descriptive mean DPPH radical-scavenging activity was higher for thesamples than for thesamples. In contrast, thesamples showed a higher mean TPC (56.3 mg GAE/g DE) than thesamples (51.5 mg GAE/g DE). Mean TFC was slightly higher in(47.7 mg CE/g DE) than in(43.5 mg CE/g DE).

These results indicate variation in DPPH radical-scavenging activity and phytochemical content among the six sampled populations. The point-level dry-extract yields, DPPH radical-scavenging activity, TPC, and TFC results are summarized in.

3.4. Species-Level Comparison of Plant Composition

To describe species-level patterns across the sampled populations, data were aggregated by calculating the mean values of the three sampling points corresponding to each species (populations P1–P3 forand P4–P6 for). The proximate and phytochemical datasets indicated contrasting biochemical profiles between the twospecies. As summarized in,had higher mean DPPH radical-scavenging activity, percentage inhibition, crude fiber, crude fat, NFE, and TFC. By contrast,had higher mean moisture, crude protein, ash, and TPC.

The contrast was particularly evident in DPPH radical-scavenging activity and ash content. Mean DPPH values were 26.4 µmol TE/g DE forand 14.7 µmol TE/g DE for, while the corresponding inhibition values were 49.0% and 21.3%, respectively. Conversely,had higher mean ash content than(15.4% and 7.06%, respectively), together with higher TPC.

The species-level descriptive comparison indicated differences in proximate composition, phytochemical content, and DPPH radical-scavenging activity between the two taxa across the studied populations.

3.5. Principal Component Analysis

PCA provided an integrated overview of the joint variation in plant biochemical traits and soil characteristics across the six studied populations. The first principal component (PC1) explained 62.52% of the total variance, whereas the second principal component (PC2) accounted for 21.83%. Together, PC1 and PC2 explained 84.35% of the total variance. The score plot (a) separated the threesampling points from the threesampling points. However, because species identity coincided with differences in sampling site, associated soil properties, and collection date, this separation describes the structure of the present dataset and cannot be interpreted as evidence of an independent taxonomic effect.

The variable loadings shown inb andindicated that positive PC1 scores were associated primarily with higher ash and crude protein contents and with higher values of several soil variables, including S, Cu, organic matter, Zn, pH, and P. Negative PC1 scores were associated with higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity, percentage inhibition, NFE, crude fat, clay content, and TFC. Accordingly, thesampling points were positioned on the positive side of PC1, whereas thesampling points were positioned on its negative side. These opposing patterns describe covariation within the present dataset and do not separate species identity from sampling site, collection period, or associated soil conditions. PC2 primarily contrasted sand, P, Zn, and TFC with CEC, TPC, clay content, pH, and Cu, indicating additional site-level variation among the six sampling points.

Within the two species-associated groups, the individual sampling points did not overlap completely, with variation along PC2 being particularly evident among thesampling points. This dispersion co-varied with differences in soil texture and nutrient status. Thesampling points also showed less pronounced site-level differentiation. Because the ordination was based on only six matched site-level observations and the design contained no comparable sampling sites at which both species were collected, the PCA could not partition the relative contributions of species identity, soil properties, collection period, or collected biomass composition. The ordination should therefore be regarded as an exploratory visualization of patterns within the present dataset rather than as evidence of independent or causal effects.

3.6. Soil-Plant Relationships

Exploratory Spearman’s rank correlation analysis performed at the sampling-point level (= 6 matched soil–plant datasets) indicated ten correlations with nominal two-sided exact permutation-values below 0.05 (;) between soil properties and plant biochemical variables. The strongest positive relationship was observed between soil Zn and crude protein (ρ = 1.000), followed by soil S and crude protein (ρ = 0.943), and soil P and crude protein (ρ = 0.943). Additional positive associations were found between soil pH and ash content (ρ = 0.899), and soil Cu and ash content (ρ = 0.886). Because the-values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons and species identity was confounded with sampling site, collection period, and associated soil conditions, these relationships should be interpreted as exploratory patterns of covariation.

Among the negative correlations, the largest absolute coefficients were observed between soil P and NFE (ρ = −0.943), soil CEC and TFC (ρ = −0.943), followed by soil pH and TFC (ρ = −0.928), soil pH and percentage inhibition (ρ = −0.899), and soil Zn and NFE (ρ = −0.886). These relationships describe opposing patterns of covariation between selected soil properties and plant traits across the six matched sampling points.

Each correlation paired one composite soil dataset with the corresponding point-level plant mean derived from a single pooled plant sample. Thus, the analysis comprised six matched site-level pairs; the three independently prepared analytical samples per sampling point characterized analytical variability and did not increase the biological sample size. The correlations cannot distinguish covariation associated with species identity from that associated with sampling site, collection period, collected biomass composition, or edaphic conditions and should not be interpreted as evidence of causal relationships.

4. Discussion

The present dataset showed coordinated variation among species grouping, biochemical traits, and site-associated soil properties across the six sampling points. The samples from the studied populations ofanddiffered in several analytical traits; however, each species was represented by different sites, associated soils, and collection dates. Consequently, the observed contrasts cannot be attributed independently to taxonomic identity, edaphic conditions, seasonal variation, or differences in the composition of the collected aerial biomass. Such combined patterns are consistent with previous reports that phytochemical variation may be associated with both taxonomic and environmental factors [,,,]. Nevertheless, the present results should be interpreted as a descriptive and hypothesis-generating comparison of the studied wild populations. Across the three sampling points representing each species, thesamples showed higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity and percentage inhibition than. Although thesamples had higher mean TPC, their DPPH radical-scavenging activity was lower, indicating that DPPH activity was not directly proportional to TPC in the present dataset. The slightly higher mean TFC recorded in thesamples may be relevant to this difference, as this species combined higher TFC with consistently higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity [,,,].

The higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity ofwas not accompanied by higher TPC, suggesting that the observed DPPH response may reflect qualitative differences in the extracted phytochemical fraction rather than total phenolic accumulation alone. Previous phytochemical investigations ofhave reported flavonoids, phenolic acids, iridoids, and other specialized metabolites with potential radical-scavenging activity [,,]. However, individual compounds were not profiled in the present study, and their contribution to the observed DPPH response cannot be determined from the available data.

By contrast, thesamples were characterized by higher mean crude protein and ash contents, together with higher mean TPC. The higher ash content in thesamples coincided with generally greater concentrations of P, S, Zn, and Cu in their associated soils. However, because the relative proportions of plant organs were not quantified and the sampling design confounded species with site, collection period, and associated soil conditions, the observed differences in ash, crude fiber, and NFE may partly reflect variation in tissue composition, maturity, and lignification. The observed profile is consistent with the ecological tendency ofto occur in nutrient-enriched habitats []. Previous studies have also characterized the biochemical composition and bioactivity of this species []. Nevertheless, the present pattern should be regarded as descriptive rather than evidence of an independent species-related difference in nutrient assimilation.

Available soil P differed markedly among the sampling points, ranging from 9 to 13 ppm at the-associated sites and reaching 323 ppm at P5, wherewas collected. This site-level contrast illustrates the close covariation between species grouping and edaphic conditions in the present dataset. However, because the two species were represented by different sites and collection periods, the observed pattern cannot demonstrate an independent species preference for particular soil P conditions or a causal association between soil P and the measured plant traits.

Anthocyanins are a widely distributed class of phenolic pigments in plants and were therefore included as an exploratory component of the present phytochemical assessment []. However, the assay responses obtained in the present study require cautious interpretation. Only trace-level signals were observed, and these were generally higher in thesamples than in thesamples. Matrix-specific limits of detection and quantification were not established, and the lowest signals showed high analytical variability. The anthocyanin responses were therefore interpreted qualitatively and excluded from quantitative species-level comparisons, PCA, and Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. Consequently, no associations between anthocyanin responses and soil properties were evaluated.

The exploratory correlation analysis showed that nutrient availability and soil reaction were associated with variation in plant composition across the six sampling points. Some of these patterns, particularly those involving crude protein, ash, TFC, and percentage inhibition, are biologically plausible in light of the established roles of mineral nutrition and soil pH in plant metabolism [,,,]. However, because the analysis was based on only six matched observations, the nominal-values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, and the soil variables co-varied with species grouping, these associations are insufficient to establish direct edaphic effects and should instead be considered hypotheses for future testing.

Among these exploratory patterns, the positive correlation between soil Zn and crude protein across the six sampling points has a plausible biochemical context, as Zn is an essential micronutrient involved in numerous enzymatic and regulatory processes related to plant metabolism, including nitrogen assimilation and protein synthesis []. In the present dataset, the-associated sampling points generally had Zn-richer soils, with soil Zn reaching 175 ppm at P5, while the corresponding plant samples also had higher crude protein contents than thesamples. Accordingly, this correlation may reflect the shared species–site structure of the dataset rather than an independent effect of soil Zn.

These relationships should not be interpreted as simple one-factor controls. The present design aligned species identity with habitat differentiation because thepopulations occurred on generally richer and more alkaline soils than thepopulations. Because habitat preference is itself a species-related ecological characteristic, the effects of taxonomic identity and edaphic context could not be separated in the present observational design. The correlations therefore likely reflect an integrated ecological signal rather than isolated mechanistic effects of individual soil variables. Similar associations between site conditions and metabolite accumulation have been reported in other medicinal plants []. This interpretation is consistent with the PCA, in which the sampling points for the two species occupied different regions of the score plot, although the analysis could not partition the respective contributions of species identity, associated soil conditions, collection period, or collected biomass composition.

Soil texture may also have been associated with these differences. The studied sites ranged from clay loam to sandy loam and sandy silt loam, implying potential differences in drainage, water availability, nutrient retention, and effective rooting conditions [,]. The two-associated sampling points with sandier soils occupied different positions in the PCA ordination, a pattern consistent with site-level variation in relation to local soil texture. Accordingly, although the independent contribution of soil texture could not be determined, the biochemical profile at each sampling point should be interpreted in relation to both the chemical and physical properties of the associated soil rather than to nutrient concentrations alone.

An important strength of the present study is the matched soil–plant design. Each plant dataset was linked directly to a soil dataset from the same sampling point, allowing phytochemical and compositional variability to be interpreted within a specific edaphic context. This approach is consistent with studies that interpret phytochemical variation within an environmental framework [,]. Another strength is the integration of multiple analytical layers, including proximate composition, DPPH radical-scavenging activity, total phenolic and flavonoid contents, qualitative anthocyanin assay responses, and a relatively broad set of soil chemical and physical variables. This multidimensional approach provides a more comprehensive descriptive assessment of the studiedpopulations and allows their biochemical profiles to be considered in relation to the associated site conditions.

The main limitation of the study is the small number of matched field populations. With only six site-level observations, the statistical analysis necessarily remains exploratory, and the observed coefficients may partly reflect species grouping or individual site effects. An additional limitation is that allpopulations were collected in May, whereas allpopulations were collected in June. Species identity was therefore completely confounded with collection period. Potential seasonal differences in temperature, solar radiation, plant water status, and soil nutrient availability could not be separated from the observed species-associated biochemical patterns. Although sampling was restricted to approximately the upper 30–40 cm of the shoots and roots were excluded, the relative proportions of stems, leaves, and reproductive structures were not separately quantified. Becauseis a scrambling annual andis a rhizomatous perennial, the collected material may still have differed in stem-to-leaf ratio, reproductive biomass, tissue age, and degree of lignification. These differences may have contributed particularly to the observed variation in ash, crude fiber, and NFE; consequently, these compositional contrasts cannot be attributed exclusively to species-related metabolism or associated soil properties. Available soil nitrogen forms, including ammonium-N (NH-N) and nitrate-N (NO-N), were not measured, and plant biomass was not quantified. The absence of soil nitrogen data is particularly relevant to the interpretation of crude protein, which was calculated from plant total nitrogen using the Kjeldahl method. For these reasons, the observed relationships should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive. This cautious interpretation is consistent with general methodological recommendations concerning effect-size interpretation and the limitations of small studies [,].

An additional analytical limitation is that the phytochemical assessment was based on bulk spectrophotometric indices, and DPPH was the only radical-scavenging assay applied. Consequently, the individual metabolites responsible for the observed responses could not be identified, and the results do not provide a comprehensive assessment of antioxidant activity. Although plant material from both species was processed using the same drying procedure, ambient drying over five days may have permitted some enzymatic oxidation of phenolic compounds and degradation of pigments. The magnitude of any such changes was not evaluated and should be considered when interpreting the observed biochemical differences. Future work should include a larger number of populations, balanced interspecific sampling across similar habitat types, repeated sampling across years and developmental stages, complementary antioxidant assays, and targeted chromatographic analyses. Such an expanded design would help distinguish species-associated patterns from environmental variation and provide a more robust basis for ecological and phytochemical generalization.

The results indicate that samples from wildandpopulations in Bulgaria differ in their biochemical profiles, while species grouping co-varied with local soil conditions. Thesamples showed higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity, whereas thesamples showed higher ash content and TPC and were collected at sites with generally higher soil nutrient levels. Trace-level anthocyanin responses were also generally higher inbut were interpreted qualitatively. These findings provide a descriptive basis for considering biochemical variation among the studied wildpopulations in relation to habitat context, including the associated soil properties [,].

5. Conclusions

The present study showed that the six sampled wild populations ofanddiffered in their biochemical profiles under the studied field conditions. Across the six sampling points, thesamples showed higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity and percentage inhibition, whereas thesamples had higher mean crude protein, ash, and TPC. The anthocyanin assay responses were detectable only at trace levels and were generally higher in thesamples. Accordingly, these observations were interpreted qualitatively and were excluded from quantitative statistical analyses.

The matched soil–plant dataset indicated that soil chemical properties, particularly pH, P, S, Zn, Cu, and CEC, co-varied with several plant biochemical traits. Integrating these paired soil–plant analytical layers provides a valuable ecological context for the biochemical variability of wild populations. The sampling points corresponding towere generally characterized by relatively nutrient-enriched and alkaline soils, whereas higher DPPH radical-scavenging activity and slightly higher mean TFC were associated with thesamples.

Because species identity coincided with specific sampling sites, collection periods, and edaphic conditions, the descriptive results, PCA ordination, and exact-permutation Spearman correlation analysis should therefore be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. They identify coordinated variation among the studied plant and soil characteristics but do not provide a basis for ranking the relative contributions of taxonomic and environmental factors or for establishing direct soil effects.

Future investigations should include larger population datasets, balanced sampling across comparable habitats, repeated observations across seasons or developmental stages, and complementary antioxidant assays. Broader comparisons involving additionalspecies would also be required before drawing conclusions about chemical variation at the genus level. Targeted analyses using high-performance liquid chromatography and liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry would allow individual phenolic acids, flavonoids, iridoids, and other metabolites to be identified and quantified and would help determine which compounds contribute to the measured DPPH radical-scavenging activity. Such studies would provide a stronger basis for distinguishing taxonomic, seasonal, and environmental sources of phytochemical variation in the two investigated species.
articles.abstract: Biochemical variation in wild medicinal plants may reflect both species-associated characteristics and habitat conditions. This study characterized six wild populations (three per species) ofL. andL. from southeastern Bulgaria using matched soil–plant sampling. Plant material was analyzed for proximate composition, total phenolic content (TPC), total flavonoid content (TFC), anthocyanin assay responses, and 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) radical-scavenging activity; associated soils were characterized for physicochemical properties, nutrient concentrations, and texture. Descriptive species-associated summaries showed thathad higher mean DPPH values (26.4 vs. 14.7 µmol Trolox equivalents per gram of dry extract), percentage inhibition (49.0% vs. 21.3%), and slightly higher TFC. Conversely,had higher mean crude protein, ash, and TPC. The anthocyanin assay produced only trace-level responses, which were generally higher inand were interpreted qualitatively. Exploratory principal component analysis showed coordinated variation in plant and soil variables and separated the two species-associated groups along the first component. Two-sided exact permutation Spearman analysis at the sampling-point level (= 6) identified nominal associations, including zinc (Zn) with crude protein (ρ = 1.000) and cation exchange capacity with TFC (ρ = −0.943). Because species identity coincided with sampling site and collection period, while aerial biomass composition was not quantified, the observed patterns cannot distinguish independent taxonomic, seasonal, and edaphic effects or support causal inference. By providing ecological context for the biochemical heterogeneity of Bulgarian populations ofand, this integrated soil–plant approach offers a descriptive, hypothesis-generating basis for further phytochemical and ecological investigations using balanced sampling across comparable habitats and collection periods.

1. Introduction

Bacteria colonize diverse human tissues, including the gastrointestinal tract and skin, and constitute a core component of the human microbiota [,]. While the majority of bacterial species are harmless—and some even play crucial roles in digestion and in limiting the growth of opportunistic pathogens—bacterial infections remain among the most common causes of disease worldwide [,]. Over recent decades, the alarming increase in antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as a major global health crisis, significantly complicating the treatment of infections caused by resistant strains [,]. The selection of effective antibiotics has become increasingly difficult [], and although new antimicrobial agents have been introduced in recent years [], resistance to many of these therapies has already been reported [,]. The rise in extensively drug-resistant (XDR) pathogens has diminished the efficacy of even the most potent antibiotics, highlighting the urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies and alternative treatment approaches [,].

In addition to AMR, oxidative stress represents another critical factor threatening human health. Oxidative stress occurs when reactive oxygen species (ROS), produced as by-products of cellular metabolism, exceed the body’s antioxidant defense capacity, leading to molecular and cellular damage []. The accumulation of ROS has been strongly linked to the pathogenesis of numerous chronic diseases, including cancer, metabolic syndrome, atherosclerosis, malaria, Alzheimer’s disease, rheumatoid arthritis, neurodegenerative disorders, and preeclampsia []. Antioxidants, which neutralize ROS and free radicals, are broadly classified as natural or synthetic compounds []. Among these, plant-derived natural antioxidants are of particular interest, as their bioactivity is influenced by factors such as plant species, cultivation conditions, and extraction or processing techniques []. Growing evidence indicates that natural compounds not only reduce oxidative stress but may also enhance immune system function []. Thus, identifying plant-based bioactive molecules with antioxidant and antimicrobial potential has become a priority in biomedical research [].

Medicinal plants have been utilized as a source of therapeutic agents for thousands of years, and it is estimated that 25–48% of currently available pharmaceuticals are derived from plants or their synthetic analogs, reflecting a growing interest in botanical resources []. The genus, a member of the Rubiaceae family, comprises roughly 1000 species globally and is represented by 101 species in Turkey [].L. (Cleavers) is an annual herbaceous plant. It flowers between April and July and occurs at altitudes ranging from 30 to 1800 m, typically in weeds, shrubs, and cultivated fields []. Ethnobotanical records indicate that the entire plant—including stems, leaves, flowers, and seeds—has long been used in folk medicine as a febrifuge, diuretic, and blood purifier to promote lymphatic circulation, and for the treatment of urinary tract infections, skin disorders such as eczema and psoriasis, ulcers, and chronic wounds. It has also been applied to alleviate swelling, infection, and inflammation, as well as to control bleeding caused by injuries [].

Previous phytochemical investigations onhave identified a diverse array of bioactive constituents, including phenolic acids (such as caffeic and p-coumaric acids), iridoids (notably asperuloside and aucubin), and various flavonoid glycosides. These compounds have been associated with a range of biological properties, particularly antioxidant and antimicrobial activities, as documented in several regional studies. While the general antimicrobial potential ofhas been explored, most prior research has focused on crude aqueous or methanolic extracts against common pathogens. However, there remains a significant gap in the literature regarding a systematic comparison of extraction solvents on its chemical profile and, more importantly, its role in disrupting bacterial communication. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first comprehensive report on the Anti-Quorum Sensing (AQS) activity of, complemented by a detailed GC-MS profiling of its ethanolic extract. By targeting the coordination of bacterial virulence rather than mere growth inhibition, this research provides a novel perspective on the therapeutic potential of this species as a sophisticated anti-virulence agent [,].

Beyond traditional bactericidal approaches, targeting bacterial virulence factors has emerged as a promising strategy to combat the global rise in antimicrobial resistance. A critical component of bacterial pathogenicity is the formation of biofilms, complex multicellular communities encased in a self-produced extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix. Biofilms play a pivotal role in chronic infections by providing a physical and metabolic barrier that renders bacteria up to 1000-fold more resistant to conventional antibiotics and host immune responses. The developmental transition from a planktonic state to a biofilm is largely regulated by Quorum Sensing (QS), a sophisticated cell-to-cell communication system based on the secretion and detection of signaling molecules. Since QS coordinates the expression of virulence genes and stabilizes the biofilm architecture, disrupting these pathways—often referred to as an anti-virulence strategy—offers a potent means to attenuate bacterial pathogenicity without exerting the selective pressure that typically leads to multi-drug resistance. Consequently, evaluating the inhibitory potential of natural products likeagainst these mechanisms is essential for developing novel therapeutic alternatives [].

The selection of extraction solvents with varying polarities—ranging from non-polar n-hexane to highly polar methanol and ethanol—is crucial for a comprehensive phytochemical evaluation, as the solubility and recovery of bioactive secondary metabolites are strictly dependent on the solvent’s dielectric constant. Despite the documented traditional uses of, a significant knowledge gap persists regarding its specific role in modulating bacterial social behaviors. To date, limited information exists regarding the antibiofilm and anti-quorum sensing potential ofextracts, and a comprehensive biochemical characterization in correlation with these advanced bioactivities remains scarce. This study is necessary now to address the urgent need for non-biocidal anti-virulence agents in the face of escalating antibiotic resistance. By systematically evaluating the influence of solvent polarity on the extraction of bioactive metabolites and linking these chemical profiles to the disruption of biofilm and quorum sensing pathways, this research aims to fill this critical void. Consequently, our findings provide a novel scientific rationale for the potential use ofas a sustainable and effective candidate for the development of next-generation anti-infective therapies.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Plant Sample

Within the scope of field studies conducted in April 2023, specimens ofwere collected from diverse ecological habitats in the Aegean Region of Türkiye. Sampling was performed on 11 April 2023, in the mountainous areas of Kavacık village, the Huzur region, and Narlıdere, specifically from understories of Turkish red pine () and black pine (). Additional surveys were carried out on 17 April 2023, in the Bozdağ region, Salihli, and Bayındır. Detailed site characteristics were recorded, including a Turkish red pine stand in Salihli–Allahdiyen (660 m altitude; 38°26′13″ N–28°05′22″ E) and an oak–Turkish red pine habitat in Bayındır (560 m altitude; 38°16′29″ N–27°39′14″ E).

The botanical authentication of the species was performed by expert biologists within the research team. A voucher specimen has been deposited at the Fauna and Flora Research and Application Center of Dokuz Eylül University with the herbarium number GA-3044. The whole plant (including aerial parts and roots) was used for the extraction process. To account for environmental variability and ensure a representative chemical profile, samples from different sites were pooled to form a composite sample. The plant materials were dried in a cool, shaded environment for three days until a constant weight was achieved and subsequently stored under controlled conditions until further analysis.

2.2. Sample Extraction Method

For the extraction of plant samples, ethanol, methanol, n-hexane, acetone, and water were selected as solvents. The choice of solvents was based on their ability to extract the most effective bioactive compounds, taking into consideration the solvent-specific extraction capacities reported by Cowan []. Since distilled water was also evaluated as a separate extraction solvent, absolute ethanol was preferred to avoid the influence of water in the ethanolic extraction system and to allow a clearer comparison among solvents of different polarities. For each extraction, 20 g of dried whole plant material was placed into individual Erlenmeyer flasks, to which 200 mL of distilled water, ethanol (99.9% purity), methanol (99.9% purity), acetone (≥99.8% purity), or n-hexane (≥99.0% purity) was added. The flasks were placed on an orbital shaker at room temperature and agitated at 160 rpm for three days. At the end of the third day, the mixtures were filtered through Whatman No. 1 filter paper. The solvents in the filtrates were evaporated using a rotary evaporator at 35–40 °C. The remaining crude extracts were weighed with an analytical balance. Following quantification, an appropriate volume of solvent was added to dissolve the dried residues, and the extracts were prepared [].

For the aqueous extract, after filtration, the samples were frozen completely at −80 °C and subsequently lyophilized to remove water. The dried residues were then weighed with an analytical balance, and distilled water was added to prepare the extracts. To ensure sterility, all extracts were passed through a 0.45 μm pore-size membrane filter prior to biological assays. For experiments conducted without the use of organic solvents, Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was employed. To minimize toxicity to microorganisms, extracts dissolved in DMSO were diluted with sterile distilled water to a final concentration of 1% DMSO.

The resulting dry extracts were reconstituted in their respective extraction solvents and subsequently diluted in a DMSO:Water (1:99,/) mixture to prepare high-concentration working stocks for biological assays. While the percentage yield was not calculated, the precise stock concentrations were determined as follows: 20.94 mg/mL for ethanol, 39.84 mg/mL for methanol, 3.97 mg/mL for acetone, and 9.11 mg/mL for n-hexane. Their corresponding final working concentrations in the DMSO:Water system were adjusted to 76.4, 276.4, 15.3, and 63.4 mg/mL, respectively. Regarding storage, the prepared extracts were kept in light-protected, airtight glass vials at 4 °C for short-term use (less than 7 days) and at −20 °C for long-term storage to maintain the stability of bioactive constituents until the completion of the bioassays.

2.3. Microorganisms and Inoculum Preparation

To evaluate the antimicrobial activities of the obtained extracts, 45 different microorganisms were selected. The study aimed to provide a comparative assessment of the extracts by maintaining a broad spectrum of test organisms. The microorganisms were obtained from the Microbiology Laboratory, Department of Biology, Faculty of Science, Dokuz Eylül University. The panel included Gram-positive bacteria, Gram-negative bacteria, and yeasts. Among the tested microorganisms, 16 were standard strains, 7 were foodborne, 11 were antibiotic-resistant strains, and 11 were clinical isolates.

The standard strains wereCECT 9111,DSM 1971,RSKK 863,ATCC 13048,ATCC 29212,ATCC 25922,ATCC 7644,DSM 50071,P1,ATCC 13076,SL1344,ATCC 25923,DSM 20044,ATCC 27844,ATCC 27836, andRSKK 184.

The foodborne isolates were,,,,,, and. The antibiotic-resistant strains weresp.,,,,,,,,MRSA,MRSA 2, and. The clinical isolates were,,,,,,2,,,, and.

Bacterial cultures were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Inoculum densities were normalized to approximately 10cfu·mLfor bacterial strains by adjusting suspensions to the 0.5 McFarland standard in 0.9% sodium chloride solution [].

2.4. Antimicrobial Activity Tests

2.4.1. Disc Diffusion Method

The antimicrobial activity ofextract was evaluated using the disk diffusion method []. Sterile 6 mm blank paper disks were impregnated with standardized volumes of the extracts (50, 100, and 150 µL), corresponding to specific mass concentrations: 1.05–3.15 mg for ethanol, 2–6 mg for methanol, 0.45–1.35 mg for n-hexane, and 0.20–0.60 mg for acetone extracts. To ensure methodological standardization, the procedures were conducted in accordance with the general principles of the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines [,]. Disks loaded only with the extraction solvents served as negative controls to verify that the observed inhibition zones were solely due to the plant metabolites and not the residual solvent. All inhibition zones were measured in millimeters (mm) following the designated incubation period. Bacterial strains were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Gentamicin and clindamycin were used () as positive controls for Gram-negative bacteria and Gram-positive bacteria, respectively.

2.4.2. Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) Assay

The broth microdilution method, as outlined by Kowalska–Krochmal and Dudek–Wicher [], was used to determine the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) in order to evaluate the antibacterial properties of theDMSO extracts. For MIC determination, the dried extracts were tested at maximum concentrations of 36,800 µg/mL for the ethanol extract, 92,130 µg/mL for the methanol extract, 5100 µg/mL for the acetone extract, and 21,130 µg/mL for the n-hexane extract, and serial dilutions were prepared in Mueller–Hinton broth. Different microbial strains were first adjusted to the turbidity of a 0.5 McFarland standard (approximately 1.5 × 10CFU/mL) and then diluted in Mueller–Hinton broth to obtain a final inoculum of approximately 5 × 10CFU/mL in each well, in accordance with CLSI recommendations []. A variety of plant extract dilutions were made and added to a 96-well plate, with 100 µL going into each well. The final volume was then increased to 150 µL by adding 50 µL of the microbial solution. Following a 24 h incubation, the MIC—the lowest concentration of the extract that fully inhibited bacterial growth—was determined through visual examination. To ensure accuracy, all tests were conducted in triplicate, and results were given in µg/mL.

2.4.3. Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC) Assay

The Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC) approach was used to find the lowest concentration of an antibiotic capable of killing a pathogenic bacterium. This assay was conducted following the MIC test. From the wells in which no visible growth was observed in the MIC assay, 10 µL was taken and streaked onto MHA plates. The inoculated bacteria were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. The lowest concentration at which no growth was observed after incubation was defined as the MBC []. To distinguish between bacteriostatic and bactericidal effects, the MBC/MIC ratio was calculated. The extract was defined as bactericidal when the MBC/MIC ≤ 4 and bacteriostatic when the MBC/MIC > 4.

2.4.4. Antibiofilm Activity Test

The antibiofilm assays were performed in 96-well polystyrene microplates. To ensure the accuracy of the results, all absorbance readings were corrected using blank wells containing only the medium and the respective extract without microbial inoculation to account for any background interference. The determination of the antibiofilm activity of plant extracts was carried out in two stages: (i) the assessment of biofilm-forming capacity and (ii) the evaluation of antibiofilm activity. In the first stage, LB Broth (Lysogeny Broth, Luria–Bertani) was dispensed into sterilized glass test tubes, and glucose monohydrate was added at six different concentrations (0%, 0.5%, 1%, 1.5%, 2%, and 2.5%). The media were subsequently re-sterilized by autoclaving. For staining the biofilms formed in microplate wells, a 0.1% crystal violet solution prepared in ethanol was used. To quantify the amount of crystal violet absorbed by the biofilms, a 3:7 acetone:ethanol mixture was applied []. For biofilm formation assays, bacterial suspensions were adjusted to 0.5 McFarland and diluted in the corresponding broth medium to obtain an initial inoculum of approximately 1 × 10CFU/mL in each well.

The bacterial strains were incubated at 37 °C and the yeasts at 27 °C for 24 or 48 h. After incubation, the microplate wells’ contents were disposed of, and planktonic cells were eliminated by washing the wells with distilled water. After drying, 200 μL of crystal violet solution was added to each well and allowed to stand for 15 min. The wells were then washed again, left to dry, and subsequently treated with an ethanol–acetone solution for 15 min. The absorbance values of the released dye were measured spectrophotometrically, enabling the determination of the appropriate glucose concentration and incubation time to be used in further assays. All experiments in this stage were performed in triplicate, with LB broth without any additives serving as the negative control [].

In the second stage, the experiment was repeated under the same conditions, with the only modification being the addition of plant extracts at ½ MIC concentrations prior to inoculation. In both the biofilm formation and antibiofilm activity assays, ethanol–acetone solutions from the treated wells were transferred to fresh microplates, and absorbance values were recorded at 550 nm using a microplate reader. 2.4.5. Antiquorum Sensing Activity Test

Pyocyanin is a blue phenazine derivative characteristic of. Upon acidification, its color changes first to yellow and then to red, while it becomes colorless under alkaline conditions. It is soluble in both water and chloroform [,]. The anti-quorum sensing activity was evaluated using thePA01 strain. To ensure that the observed reduction in pyocyanin production was specifically due to the disruption of quorum sensing pathways and not a consequence of growth suppression, bacterial growth was monitored by measuring the optical density at 600 nm (OD) throughout the incubation period. Only extracts that did not significantly inhibit planktonic growth at the tested concentrations were evaluated for pyocyanin inhibition. To assess the inhibitory effect of plant extracts on pyocyanin pigment production, 100 μL of the extract was added to LB broth along with a bacterial culture adjusted to OD= 0.05, followed by incubation at 37 °C with shaking for 9 h. Subsequently, the cultures were further incubated with shaking at 37 °C for 24 h. At the end of the incubation period, 5 mL of chloroform was added to the culture medium and vortexed for 30 s. The separated chloroform phase (2 mL) was transferred into glass tubes, to which 1 mL of an HCl–HO mixture (0.2 mmol) was added and vortexed for 30 s. The resulting pink phase formed at the top of the tubes was measured spectrophotometrically at 520 nm. All experiments were conducted in triplicate. 2.5. Antioxidant Activity Test

The antioxidant potential of theethanol extract was evaluated across a concentration range of 0.00781 to 1 mg/mL using for 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH). For the DPPH assay, the IC50 values were calculated using a four-parameter log-logistic (4PL) non-linear regression model to ensure precise estimation of the dose–response relationship. The results for DPPH and ABTS were expressed as percentage inhibition, while the reducing capacities in CUPRAC and FRAP assays were quantified as Ascorbic Acid Equivalents (AAE) based on standardized calibration curves. Procedural descriptions followed established protocols.

2.5.1. 2,2-Diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) Assay

The antioxidant potential ofwas determined through the DPPH free radical scavenging assay. This widely applied method assesses the capability of antioxidant molecules present in plant extracts to quench stable free radicals. For the preparation of the working solution, DPPH was dissolved in ethanol and kept in a dark environment to maintain its stability and prevent photodecomposition []. Subsequently, different concentrations of the extracts were mixed with the DPPH solution in a 96-well microplate. After incubation for 30 min at ambient temperature under dark conditions, the absorbance was recorded at 515 nm using a Microplate Spectrophotometer (Biotek, Winooski, VT, USA). Ascorbic acid was utilized as a reference antioxidant for comparison purposes.

2.5.2. Ferric Reducing Antioxidant Power (FRAP) Assay

The ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) ofextract was determined according to the protocol described by Benzie et al. [], with minor adjustments. Three stock solutions were prepared: acetate buffer, TPTZ solution, and FeCl·6HO. In the assay procedure, 2.9 mL of the reagent was mixed with 0.1 mL of the plant extract, resulting in the formation of an intense blue complex due to the reduction of Feto Fe. The reaction mixtures were kept at room temperature in darkness for 90 min before recording the absorbance at 593 nm. All analyses were conducted in triplicate. Ascorbic acid served as the standard antioxidant reference, while the solvent mixed with FRAP reagent functioned as the negative control.

2.5.3. Cupric Reducing Antioxidant Capacity (CUPRAC) Assay

The cupric reducing antioxidant capacity (CUPRAC) of the extracts was evaluated based on the method proposed by Apak et al. [], with slight modifications. The stock solutions included CuCl·2HO, neocuproine in methanol, and ammonium acetate buffer. For each assay, equal volumes (1 mL) of CuCl·2HO, neocuproine, and ammonium acetate buffer were combined with 1 mL of the plant extract. The reaction mixtures were then incubated for 90 min at room temperature in the dark. The appearance of a yellow color indicated the reduction of Cu(II) to Cu(I). Absorbance was subsequently recorded at 450 nm. All determinations were performed in triplicate. Ascorbic acid was used as the positive control, whereas the extraction solvent alone was used as the negative control.

2.5.4. 2,2′-Azino-bis(3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid) (ABTS) Assay

The ABTS radical scavenging capacity was assessed following the procedures outlined by Miller and Rice-Evans [] and Re et al. []. The ABTS•radical cation was produced by reacting ABTS solution with potassium persulfate in equal volumes (1:1,/), followed by incubation in the dark for 12–16 h. The resulting solution was diluted with methanol to obtain an absorbance of 0.700 ± 0.05 at 734 nm. For the assay, 2 mL of the ABTS•working solution was mixed with 1 mL of the plant extract, and the mixture was incubated for 90 min at room temperature. Absorbance readings were then recorded at 734 nm. Each test was performed in triplicate, with ascorbic acid serving as positive control and methanol as the negative control.

2.6. Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectroscopy Method (GC-MS)

Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS) was employed to identify and quantify the biochemical constituents present in the ethanol, methanol,-hexane and acetone extracts of. The GC-MS analyses were carried out using Agilent GC 8890 and Agilent GC/MSD 5977B with HP-5 MS column (Santa Clara, CA, USA). The analytical procedure and instrumental parameters adhered to the methodology established by Simsek et al. []. The mass spectrometer was operated in positive electron impact (EI+) mode at 70 eV ionization energy, with a scan range of 42–650and a cycle time of 0.5 s. The MS transfer line, interface, and ion source temperatures were maintained at 280 °C, 280 °C, and 230 °C, respectively. All peaks were quantified based on peak area. Compound identification was performed by matching the observed retention times (RT) and MS fragmentation patterns with those in the Wiley-Nist MS library and established literature data (Hoboken, NJ, USA).

2.7. Statistics

Statistical analyses were conducted using R Studio (2025.09.1). To ensure data reliability, antimicrobial activity and all other biological assays were performed as three independent experiments, each containing internal technical replicates. The Shapiro–Wilk test was used to verify the normality of the data, and Levene’s test was applied to assess the homogeneity of variances. Differences between experimental groups (solvents and concentrations) were evaluated using one-way or two-way ANOVA, followed by Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference (HSD) post hoc test for multiple comparisons. While ANOVA was primarily utilized to determine the significance of differences between treatment groups, the lack of significant variance among parallel replicates was used to confirm the reproducibility of the experimental measurements. Pearson’s correlation coefficient was calculated to examine the relationship between extract concentration and corresponding biological activities, as well as the association between antioxidant capacity and phenolic/flavonoid content. All statistical analyses were performed at a 95% confidence level, with< 0.05 considered statistically significant.
